segments: ... and the yokes of the Arab kings {OCR?}.
Mosul, after the murder of his deputy Nasir al-Din,
he went to Aleppo because it belonged to him,
and he gathered an army and went and encamped against the fortress of Qal'at Ja'bar.
And one day, while he was sitting in his tent,
and craftsmen had forged a gold basin for him,
and when they brought it before him,
and he bent his head down and was gazing at it,
one of the slaves who bore his weapons struck him with a sword from behind him,
and cut off his head.
Others, however, say
that at night, while he was drowned in sleep in drunkenness,
three of his slaves killed him,
and fled beneath the wall,
and said to the watchmen:
"Draw us up, that we may give you good tidings."
And they let down a basket to them,
and brought them up one by one with a rope.
And when they went up, they said {OCR?} to the garrison of the fortress:
"We have now killed Zangi,
and no one is aware of it yet.
So make it known to them yourselves!"
Then they sounded horns and shouted down to those below, saying:
"Arise, bury your master who has been killed,
before he stinks!"
And when they went in to Zangi,
they found him slaughtered.
Now Mahmud, his son, who was called Nur al-Din,
because he was with him,
pressed the fortress even harder in battle.
And when they grew weary of fighting,
both he and those within,
he said to them:
"Surrender the killers of my father to me,
and you shall have peace."
And they surrendered those three slaves to him.
And after cruel tortures, he put them to death,
and burned their corpses.
Now to Zangi, there remained after him four sons
and one daughter:
Sayf al-Din Ghazi,
Nur al-Din Mahmud,
Qutb al-Din Mawdud,
and Nusrat al-Din Amir-Amiran,
and their sister.
For Zangi built the royal palaces that are in Mosul,
inasmuch as before him there was only one royal palace in it,
that which was opposite the stadium, that is,
the Maydan;
and he raised its walls
and deepened its moat.
And he opened the gate which is called 'Imadi after his name.
He also planted gardens round about it.
It is said
that previously,
melons and grapes were so scarce in Mosul
that when a shopkeeper weighed grapes to sell,
he would cut the cluster with scissors,
being careful lest a single grape fall to the ground.
